monthly_review.summary: This month shows increased volume and strategic HR zone distribution, with notable gains in aerobic efficiency and cadence consistency, though pace slowed slightly compared to last month.
monthly_review.highlight: Aerobic efficiency improved from 13.28 to 13.49 m/sec per bpm — the strongest positive shift this month, indicating better oxygen utilization at given heart rates.

goal_tracker.message: You’ve already exceeded last month’s total distance (35.6 km vs 32.9 km) and number of runs (8 vs 7). No additional running is needed to match last month — focus instead on quality and recovery over the remaining 2 days.

insights.title: Improved oxygen economy despite slower average pace
insights.body: Aerobic efficiency rose from 13.28 to 13.49 m/sec per bpm — a +0.21 gain — even as avg pace slowed by 6 sec/km. This suggests enhanced cardiovascular efficiency, likely supported by increased Z1–Z2 time (Z1 up from 4% to 24% this month) and consistent sub-threshold work.

insights.title: Strategic shift toward foundational aerobic development
insights.body: Z1 time jumped from 4% to 24% while Z2 remained high (31%), reducing reliance on Z3 (down from 36% to 24%). This reflects a deliberate move toward base-building — aligning with improved aerobic TE (+0.1) and VO2 max stability (35.0 in 3 recent runs vs 34.0 in April 12 run).

insights.title: Cadence variability signals pacing inconsistency and fatigue management opportunities
insights.body: Cadence dropped sharply to 87 spm during the 14:00/km run on Apr 26 (HR 120 bpm), far below your typical 146–150 spm range — suggesting form breakdown at very low intensity, possibly due to fatigue or lack of neuromuscular engagement. Meanwhile, stride length fluctuated widely (72.88–91.78 cm), correlating with pace and HR changes.

insights.title: High aerobic TE sessions concentrated late in the month
insights.body: Three of your four highest aerobic TE runs (>4.0) occurred in the last 17 days (Apr 12: TE 4.6; Apr 22: TE 3.1; Apr 28: TE 2.5), with Apr 12 being the standout (TE 4.6, HR 163 bpm, pace 7:25/km). This clustering may limit recovery — especially given only 2 rest days between those efforts.

recommendations.action: Do a 45-minute Zone 2 run tomorrow (May 1) at HR ≤135 bpm, focusing on maintaining cadence ≥145 spm throughout — use metronome or audio cue if needed.
recommendations.reason: Your recent Zone 2 runs show cadence dropping when pace slows (e.g., Apr 26: 87 spm at 14:00/km); reinforcing neuromuscular patterning at sustainable HR will stabilize stride efficiency and support aerobic efficiency gains.

recommendations.action: Replace one upcoming run with a 20-minute barefoot or minimalist-shoe drill session: 4 × (30-sec high-knee march + 30-sec butt-kick + 30-sec A-skip), followed by 5 minutes of cadence-focused jogging at 150 spm on grass.
recommendations.reason: Cadence declined from 150 spm (Mar) to 142 spm (Apr) overall, and ground contact time remains elevated (298–327 ms) versus elite recreational norms (<280 ms); neuromuscular drills improve turnover efficiency without adding load.

recommendations.action: Perform a 10-minute post-run mobility routine tonight: 3 min foam rolling quads/hamstrings, 2 min calf rocking on tennis ball, 5 min dynamic hip flexor + glute activation (fire hydrants, clamshells).
recommendations.reason: Ground contact time increased to 327 ms on Apr 26 (vs 298 ms on Apr 22) and vertical oscillation varied widely (6.4–8.8 cm), suggesting emerging fatigue or reduced elastic recoil — mobility work supports tissue resilience and stride consistency.

weekly_focus.description: Prioritize cadence control, ground contact efficiency, and stride rhythm across all runs — not just speed — to lock in recent aerobic efficiency gains and prevent form decay under fatigue.
suggested_sessions: Zone 2 tempo run with cadence target (145–150 spm)
Short interval run: 6 × 90-sec @ goal 5K pace (428 sec/km), strict 150 spm focus
